Infinite chains in the tree of numerical semigroups

Mariana Rosas-Ribeiro ††thanks: Electronic address: mariana.rosas@urv.cat; Corresponding author Affiliation: Department of Computer Engineering and Mathematics,
Universitat Rovira i Virgili,
Tarragona, Spain    Maria Bras-Amorós ††thanks: Electronic address: maria.bras@upc.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics,
Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya,
Barcelona, Spain
January 29, 2024
Abstract

One major problem in the study of numerical semigroups is determining the growth of the semigroup tree. In the present work, infinite chains of numerical semigroups in the semigroup tree, firstly introduced by Bras-Amorós and Bulygin (Semigroup Forum, 71:561–574, 2009), are studied. Computational results show that these chains are rare, but without them the tree would not be infinite. It is proved that for each genus g≥5g\geq 5 there are more semigroups of that genus not belonging to infinite chains than semigroups belonging. Bras-Amorós and Bulygin (Semigroup Forum, 71:561–574, 2009) presented a characterization of the semigroups that belong to infinite chains in terms of the coprimality of the left elements of the semigroup as well as a result on the cardinality of the set of infinite chains to which a numerical semigroup belongs in terms of the primality of the greatest common divisor of these left elements. We revisit these results and fix an imprecision on the cardinality of the set of infinite chains to which a semigroup belongs in the case when the greatest common divisor of the left elements is a prime number. We then look at infinite chains in subtrees with fixed multiplicity. When the multiplicity is a prime number there is only one infinite chain in the tree of semigroups with such multiplicity. When the multiplicity is 44 or 66 we prove a self-replication behavior in the subtree and prove a formula for the number of semigroups in infinite chains of a given genus and multiplicity 44 and 66, respectively.

Keywords— numerical semigroups; semigroup tree; infinite chains

1 Introduction

A numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda is a subset of the non-negative integers ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0}, containing 00, closed under addition and with finite complement in ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0}. The elements of ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} that are not in Λ\Lambda are called the gaps and the number of gaps is the genus g⁡(Λ)g(\Lambda) of the numerical semigroup. Intuitively, the possibilities of obtaining numerical semigroups with gg gaps seem to increase as the number gg increases and indeed computational results have shown this ([2], [7]). It was conjectured in [2], 2008, that the sequence ngn_{g} formed by the number of numerical semigroups of each genus gg, not only is increasing but also grows like the Fibonacci sequence. In 2012, one such conjecture was proved [9], namely ngφg→g→∞S\dfrac{n_{g}}{\varphi^{g}}\xrightarrow{g\to\infty}S, where φ\varphi is the golden ratio and SS is at least 3.783.78. It remains unproved that ng−2+ng−1≤ngn_{g-2}+n_{g-1}\leq n_{g}; even the weaker conjecture that ng−1≤ngn_{g-1}\leq n_{g}, already announced in 2007 [1], remains open.

One way to label all elements of the numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda is to enumerate them. The enumeration λ\lambda of a numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda is the unique increasing bijection between ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} and Λ\Lambda, and we denote by λi\lambda_{i} the image of i∈ℕ0i\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. In particular, λ0=0\lambda_{0}=0. The multiplicity of Λ\Lambda is m⁡(Λ)=λ1m(\Lambda)=\lambda_{1}. It holds m⁡(Λ)≤g⁡(Λ)+1m(\Lambda)\leq g(\Lambda)+1. The conductor of Λ\Lambda is c⁡(Λ)=λkc(\Lambda)=\lambda_{k}, where λk+n∈Λ\lambda_{k}+n\in\Lambda for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and λk−1∉Λ\lambda_{k}-1\notin\Lambda. The number c⁡(Λ)−1c(\Lambda)-1 is the largest gap and is called the Frobenius number of Λ\Lambda and denoted by F⁡(Λ)F(\Lambda). The elements of Λ\Lambda that are smaller than its conductor are the left elements, denoted by ℒ⁡(Λ)\mathcal{L}(\Lambda).

Let [a,∞)[a,\infty) stand for {i∈ℕ0:i≥a}\{i\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}:i\geq a\}. Numerical semigroups of the form {0}∪[λ1,∞)\{0\}\cup[\lambda_{1},\infty) are called ordinary and those of the form {2​n:n≥0}∪[λk,∞),λk\{2n:n\geq 0\}\cup[\lambda_{k},\infty),\ \lambda_{k} even, are called hyperelliptic semigroups.

It is well known that each numerical semigroup has a unique minimal system of generators. The cardinality of the minimal system of generators is called the embedding dimension of Λ\Lambda and we denote it by e⁡(Λ)e(\Lambda). In view of the fact that two generators cannot lie in the same congruence class modulo m⁡(Λ)m(\Lambda), one has e⁡(Λ)≤λ1e(\Lambda)\leq\lambda_{1}. The minimal generators of Λ\Lambda that are not in ℒ⁡(Λ)\mathcal{L}(\Lambda) are the effective generators or right generators of Λ\Lambda and with them we can organize the collection of all numerical semigroups in a tree rooted at ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0}. In Figure 1 one can see the tree with the nodes of level at most 6.

In this representation, the elements in orange are the effective generators. That tree is constructed by removing one by one the effective generators from each numerical semigroup. In this way, the level of the tree is equal to the genus of the numerical semigroups that are at that level (assume that the root has level zero). For more details of this tree, we suggest consulting [3], [9] and [7]. From the tree perspective, numerical semigroups can also be seen as nodes. In this way the children of a numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda are those numerical semigroups that are obtained by taking away one right generator from Λ\Lambda. Conversely, the parent of a numerical semigroup is obtained by adding its Frobenius number (the parent is one level lower in the tree). The number of children of a node Λ\Lambda is called its efficacy and is denoted by h⁡(Λ)h(\Lambda). By the previous remarks, one can deduce that h⁡(Λ)≤e⁡(Λ)≤m⁡(Λ)≤g⁡(Λ)+1h(\Lambda)\leq e(\Lambda)\leq m(\Lambda)\leq g(\Lambda)+1. As can be seen in the references cited above, this tree has been used to study the growth of the ngn_{g} sequence.

Every numerical semigroup of genus larger than g⁡(Λ)g(\Lambda) connected to Λ\Lambda through edges in the tree is said to be a descendant of Λ\Lambda. A node that has no descendants is said to be a leaf and a node that has exactly one child is said to be a stick. An infinite set of numerical semigroups is said to be an infinite chain if it contains ℕ0{\mathbb{N}}_{0} and the semigroups in the set can be enumerated in such a way that each one is the parent of the next one.

The set of ordinary semigroups and the set of hyperelliptic semigroups each form an infinite chain and, as we will see throughout this paper, these two chains are well positioned in the numerical semigroup tree.

Infinite chains of numerical semigroups were first investigated in [5]. This reference presented a characterization of the semigroups that belong to infinite chains in terms of the coprimality of the left elements of the semigroup as well as a result on the number of infinite chains to which a numerical semigroup belongs in terms of the primality of the greatest common divisor of these left elements.

In Section 2 we state some preliminary results and in Section 3 we revisit the main result of [5] and fix an imprecision on the cardinality of the set of infinite chains to which a semigroup belongs in the case when the greatest common divisor of the left elements is a prime number. The resulting fixed theorem is Theorem 3.4.

Computational results show that infinite chains are rare, but without them the tree would not be infinite. For this reason, we direct the study on infinite chains in order to investigate the broader problem of the tree growth. In Section 4 we prove that for each genus g≥5g\geq 5 there are more semigroups of that genus not belonging to infinite chains than semigroups belonging (Theorem 4.10).

Another aspect that is evident in the tree is that semigroups of the same multiplicity form subtrees. In Section 5 we look at infinite chains in subtrees with fixed multiplicity. When the multiplicity is a prime number, one can prove, as a consequence of Theorem 3.4, that there is only one infinite chain in the tree of semigroups with such multiplicity. For the cases of multiplicity 44 and multiplicity 66, we prove a self-replication behavior in the subtree formed by the semigroups with fixed multiplicity equal to 44 and that are in infinite chains (Subsection 5.2); and a different self-replication behavior in the subtree formed by the semigroups with fixed multiplicity equal to 66 and that are in infinite chains (Subsection 5.3). This enables us to prove a formula for the amount of semigroups of genus gg that belong to infinite chains, of any given prime multiplicity (Theorem 5.3), of multiplicity 44 (Theorem 5.4), or of multiplicity 66 (Theorem 5.12).

2 Preliminary results

The next lemma was proved in [3] but we enunciate it here in a different way, underlying the result used in the original proof. Among other things, it allows to study the children of the children, or grandchildren, of most numerical semigroups.

Lemma 2.1 ([5], Lemma 1).

If λi1<λi2<⋯<λin\lambda_{i_{1}}<\lambda_{i_{2}}<\dots<\lambda_{i_{n}} are the effective generators of a non-ordinary numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda, then the effective generators of Λ∖{λij}\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda_{i_{j}}\} are either λij+1,…,λin\lambda_{i_{j+1}},\dots,\lambda_{i_{n}} or λij+1,…,λin,λij+λ1\lambda_{i_{j+1}},\dots,\lambda_{i_{n}},\lambda_{i_{j}}+\lambda_{1}.

Our next proposition gives a bound for the maximum effective generator.

Proposition 2.2.

Every effective generator is at most the conductor plus the multiplicity minus one.

Proof.

Indeed, for a numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda, if a≥c⁡(Λ)+m⁡(Λ)a\geq c(\Lambda)+m(\Lambda), then a=m⁡(Λ)+(a−m⁡(Λ))a=m(\Lambda)+(a-m(\Lambda)), with both m⁡(Λ)m(\Lambda) and a−m⁡(Λ)a-m(\Lambda) nongaps. ∎

The last preliminary result is a characterization of ordinary semigroups by the number of children in terms of the genus.

Lemma 2.3.

If a numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda with genus gg has g+1g+1 children, then Λ\Lambda is ordinary.

Proof.

The following sequence of inequalities must indeed be a sequence of equalities:

g+1=h⁡(Λ)≤e⁡(Λ)≤m⁡(Λ)≤g+1.g+1=h(\Lambda)\leq e(\Lambda)\leq m(\Lambda)\leq g+1.

Hence, m⁡(Λ)=g+1m(\Lambda)=g+1, meaning that all gaps of Λ\Lambda are smaller than m⁡(Λ)m(\Lambda), and, hence, Λ\Lambda must be ordinary. ∎

3 Infinite chains

In this section we are interested in studying the nodes of the tree of numerical semigroups that have infinitely many descendants. An infinite chain is a sequence of semigroups Λ0,Λ1,Λ2,…\Lambda_{0},\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2},\dots such that Λ0=ℕ0\Lambda_{0}=\mathbb{N}_{0} and Λi\Lambda_{i} is the parent of Λi+1\Lambda_{i+1} in the semigroup tree. Notice that a numerical semigroup belongs to an infinite chain if and only if it has infinitely many descendants.

First, we analyze which nodes in the semigroup tree have an infinite number of descendants. For the nodes having a finite number of descendants we give a way to determine the descendant at largest distance; for the nodes having an infinite number of descendants we determine the number of infinite chains in which the semigroup lies. It turns out here that primality and coprimality of integers appear in the scene as discriminating factors.

Let 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} be the set of all numerical semigroups, and let 𝕀{\mathbb{I}} be the set of all infinite chains. One element of 𝕀{\mathbb{I}} contains infinitely many elements in 𝕊{\mathbb{S}}. As an example, the sequence of ordinary semigroups, 𝒪g={0,g+1,→}{\mathcal{O}}_{g}=\{0,g+1,\rightarrow\} for any g∈ℕ0g\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}, is in 𝕀{\mathbb{I}}. We denote it I𝒪I_{\mathcal{O}}. That is,

I𝒪={𝒪g:g≥0}.{I_{\mathcal{O}}}=\{{\mathcal{O}}_{g}:g\geq 0\}.

Another example is the sequence of hyperelliptic semigroups, ℋg={0,2,4,…,2g,→}{\mathcal{H}}_{g}=\{0,2,4,\dots,2g,\rightarrow\}. We denote it IℋI_{\mathcal{H}}. That is,

Iℋ={ℋg:g≥0}.{I_{\mathcal{H}}}=\{{\mathcal{H}}_{g}:g\geq 0\}.

Each element in 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} may be contained in none, one, several, or infinitely many elements of 𝕀{\mathbb{I}}. The aim of this section is analyzing what circumstances give what of these cases. Then, we analyze what kind of generators appear in infinite chains.

For the proof of the next lemma we use that the integers ℓ1,…,ℓm\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{m} generate a numerical semigroup if and only if they are coprime.

Lemma 3.1.

Given an infinite chain I=(Λi)i≥0I=(\Lambda_{i})_{i\geq 0} different than I𝒪I_{\mathcal{O}}, it holds that

⋂i≥0Λi=d⋅Λ\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i}=d\cdot\Lambda

for some integer d>1d>1 and some numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda.

Proof.

The intersection ⋂i≥0Λi\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i} satisfies 0∈⋂i≥0Λi0\in\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i}. Since there exists a non-ordinary semigroup in II, there must be a non-zero element x∈⋂i≥0Λix\in\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i} and x+y∈⋂i≥0Λix+y\in\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i} for all x,y∈⋂i≥0Λix,y\in\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i}.

Furthermore, all elements in ⋂i≥0Λi\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i} must be divisible by an integer d>1d>1. Indeed, otherwise we could find a finite set of coprime elements which would generate a numerical semigroup, and this numerical semigroup should be a subset of ⋂i≥0Λi\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i}. Then the infinite chain would not contain any semigroup with genus larger than that of this semigroup, giving a contradiction. Let dd be the greatest of the common divisors of ⋂i≥0Λi\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i}. Then 1d​(⋂i≥0Λi)\frac{1}{d}\left(\bigcap_{i\geq 0}\Lambda_{i}\right) must be a numerical semigroup. ∎

Lemma 3.2.

Given an integer d>1d>1 and a numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda, the infinite chain obtained by deleting repetitions in the sequence Λj=d⋅Λ∪{ℓ∈ℕ:ℓ≥j}\Lambda_{j}=d\cdot\Lambda\cup\{\ell\in{\mathbb{N}}:\ell\geq j\} has intersection d⋅Λd\cdot\Lambda.

Consequently, 𝕀∖I𝒪{\mathbb{I}}\setminus I_{\mathcal{O}} and ℕ≥2×𝕊{\mathbb{N}}_{\geq 2}\times{\mathbb{S}} are in a one-to-one correspondence. For example, in this correspondence, the image of IℋI_{\mathcal{H}} would be (2,ℕ0)(2,{\mathbb{N}}_{0}).

Remark 3.3.

Any ordinary numerical semigroup belongs to infinitely many infinite chains. Indeed, {0,m,→}\{0,m,\rightarrow\} belongs, among others to ω⁡(m′,ℕ0)\omega(m^{\prime},{\mathbb{N}}_{0}) for any m′≥mm^{\prime}\geq m.

In the next theorem we show that the greatest common divisor of the left elements of a non-ordinary numerical semigroup determines whether the numerical semigroup has an infinite number of descendants. We say that a descendant of a numerical semigroup is a descendant beyond a given element aa of its parent if it contains all semigroup elements of the parent up to aa. For example, {0,4,5,8,9,10,12,→}\{0,4,5,8,9,10,12,\rightarrow\} and {0,4,5,6,8,→}\{0,4,5,6,8,\rightarrow\} are descendants of {0,4,→}\{0,4,\rightarrow\}, but only {0,4,5,6,8,→}\{0,4,5,6,8,\rightarrow\} is a descendant beyond 66.

We use the fact that a finite number of coprime elements generate a numerical semigroup.

Theorem 3.4.

Let Λ\Lambda be a non-ordinary numerical semigroup with enumeration λ\lambda, genus gg, and conductor cc, and let dd be the greatest common divisor of ℒ⁡(Λ)\mathcal{L}(\Lambda). Then,

  1. a.

    Λ\Lambda lies in an infinite chain if and only if d≠1d\neq 1.

  2. b.

    If d=1d=1, then the descendant of Λ\Lambda with largest genus is the numerical semigroup generated by the non-zero elements of ℒ⁡(Λ)\mathcal{L}(\Lambda), that is, the numerical semigroup generated by λ1,…,λc−g−1\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{c-g-1}.

  3. c.

    If d≠1d\neq 1 and dd is not prime, then Λ\Lambda lies in infinitely many infinite chains.

  4. d.

    If dd is a prime, then the number of infinite chains in which Λ\Lambda lies is one plus the number of descendants of Λ/d:={0,λ1d,…,λc−g−1d}∪{ℓ∈ℕ0:ℓ≥⌈cd⌉}\Lambda/d:=\{0,\frac{\lambda_{1}}{d},\dots,\frac{\lambda_{c-g-1}}{d}\}\cup\{\ell\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}:\ell\geq\lceil\frac{c}{d}\rceil\} beyond λc−g−1d\frac{\lambda_{c-g-1}}{d}.

Now, each descendant of Λ\Lambda must contain Λ′\Lambda^{\prime}. Thus, the maximum of the genera of the descendants of Λ\Lambda is the genus of Λ′\Lambda^{\prime}, which is finite, and so there is no infinite chain containing Λ\Lambda.

    On the other hand, if d≠1d\neq 1 and c−g−1≥2c-g-1\geq 2, then

    As we have seen in the previous statement, the semigroup Λ′\Lambda^{\prime}, which is a descendant itself of Λ\Lambda, must be contained in each descendant of Λ\Lambda.

4 Minority of semigroups in infinite chains

In this section we prove that for each fixed genus g≥5g\geq 5 the majority of semigroups do not belong to any infinite chain.

From the characterization given by Theorem 3.4 of the semigroups that are in infinite chains, we are able to investigate which children of such semigroups remain in infinite chains.

Corollary 4.1.

If the numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda lies in an infinite chain, then it has at most two children in infinite chains.

Proof.

Let Λ\Lambda be a numerical semigroup belonging to an infinite chain, cc its conductor, ℒ⁡(Λ)\mathcal{L}(\Lambda) its set of left elements and d=gcd​(ℒ​(Λ))d=\text{gcd}(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda)). By Theorem 3.4, d≠1d\neq 1 and by definition an effective generator of Λ\Lambda is c+ic+i for some i≥0i\geq 0. So every child of Λ\Lambda is of the type Λ∖{c+i}\Lambda\setminus\{c+i\} for some i≥0i\geq 0 and the left elements of this child are either ℒ⁡(Λ∖{c})=ℒ⁡(Λ)\mathcal{L}(\Lambda\setminus\{c\})=\mathcal{L}(\Lambda), if i=0i=0, or ℒ⁡(Λ∖{c+i})=ℒ⁡(Λ)∪{c,…,c+i−1}\mathcal{L}(\Lambda\setminus\{c+i\})=\mathcal{L}(\Lambda)\cup\{c,\dots,c+i-1\}, if i>0i>0. Now, suppose i≥2i\geq 2. This implies ℒ⁡(Λ∖{c+i})⊇{c,c+1}\mathcal{L}(\Lambda\setminus\{c+i\})\supseteq\{c,c+1\} and, since gcd(c,c+1)=1(c,c+1)=1, we have gcd(ℒ⁡(Λ∖{c+i}))=1(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda\setminus\{c+i\}))=1. So, Λ∖{c+i}\Lambda\setminus\{c+i\}, for i≥2i\geq 2, does not have infinitely many descendants. ∎

Remark 4.2.

The proof above makes it clear that the only children of a semigroup Λ\Lambda that may have infinitely many descendants are Λ∖{c⁡(Λ)}\Lambda\setminus\{c(\Lambda)\} and Λ∖{c⁡(Λ)+1}\Lambda\setminus\{c(\Lambda)+1\}.

Proposition 4.3.

Except for ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} and hyperelliptic semigroups, every numerical semigroup that is in an infinite chain has at least one child that is not.

Proof.

Let Λ\Lambda be a numerical semigroup such that gcd​(ℒ​(Λ))≠1\text{gcd}(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda))\neq 1. Suppose that Λ\Lambda only has children that are in infinite chains. Let c=c⁡(Λ)c=c(\Lambda). By Corollary 4.1, the set of effective generators is either {c}\{c\}, {c+1}\{c+1\}, or {c,c+1}\{c,c+1\}.

In the first case, the only child of Λ\Lambda is Λ1=Λ∖{c}\Lambda_{1}=\Lambda\setminus\{c\} and, since Λ\Lambda is in an infinite chain, Λ1\Lambda_{1} cannot be a leaf. By Lemma 2.1, Λ1\Lambda_{1} has a (unique) effective generator which is c+mc+m, where m=m⁡(Λ)m=m(\Lambda). So, the child of Λ1\Lambda_{1} is Λ2=Λ1∖{c+m}=Λ∖{c,c+m}\Lambda_{2}=\Lambda_{1}\setminus\{c+m\}=\Lambda\setminus\{c,c+m\}. If m>2m>2 then, as cc is the conductor of Λ\Lambda, we have {c+1,c+2}⊂Λ∖{c,c+m}=Λ2\{c+1,c+2\}\subset\Lambda\setminus\{c,c+m\}=\Lambda_{2}. However, since Λ2\Lambda_{2} is the only child of the only child of Λ\Lambda, it must also be in an infinite chain. That is, gcd(ℒ⁡(Λ2))≠1(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda_{2}))\neq 1 but gcd(c+1,c+2)=1(c+1,c+2)=1, a contradiction.

Similarly, in the second case if the only effective generator of Λ\Lambda is c+1c+1, then all its descendants are sticks, the next ones being Λ1=Λ∖{c+1}\Lambda_{1}=\Lambda\setminus\{c+1\} and Λ2=Λ1∖{c+1+m}=Λ∖{c+1,c+1+m}\Lambda_{2}=\Lambda_{1}\setminus\{c+1+m\}=\Lambda\setminus\{c+1,c+1+m\}. And if m>2m>2, {c+2,c+3}⊂Λ2\{c+2,c+3\}\subset\Lambda_{2}, contradicting gcd(ℒ⁡(Λ2))≠1(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda_{2}))\neq 1.

Finally, for the third case we assume that cc and c+1c+1 are the only effective generators of Λ\Lambda. So, when we take out c+1c+1 we are in the same situation as in the second case, where we need m≤2m\leq 2.

Therefore the only possibility for Λ\Lambda to have all children in infinite chains is if the multiplicity of Λ\Lambda is equal to 11 or 22, that is, if Λ\Lambda is ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} or a hyperelliptic semigroup. ∎

A direct conclusion from Proposition 4.3 is that, with the exception of ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} and hyperelliptic semigroups, a numerical semigroup that is in an infinite chain has at least two children.

The way the tree of numerical semigroups is constructed generates subtrees of numerical semigroups with the same multiplicity. We will comment more on this in the next section. For now, consider the following result.

Lemma 4.4.

For every pair (g,m),g≥1,2≤m≤g+1,(g,m),g\geq 1,2\leq m\leq g+1, there exists a numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda with g⁡(Λ)=gg(\Lambda)=g that lies in an infinite chain formed by numerical semigroups of multiplicity mm.

Proof.

Consider the chain ω⁡(m,ℕ0)\omega(m,{\mathbb{N}}_{0}) in the notation of Lemma 3.2 and note that, starting from {0,m,→}\{0,m,\rightarrow\}, all semigroups in this chain have multiplicity mm, and since they form an unbroken path in the tree, they achieve all genera g≥m−1g\geq m-1. ∎

Lemma 4.5.

Let Λ\Lambda be a numerical semigroup with enumeration λ\lambda, genus gg, conductor cc, and gcd(ℒ⁡(Λ))=d>1(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda))=d>1. Then the number of children of Λ\Lambda is at least d−1d-1 and if λ1=d\lambda_{1}=d, then the number of children of Λ\Lambda is exactly d−1d-1.

Proof.

Since dd is a divisor of the left elements of Λ\Lambda, we have d≤λ1d\leq\lambda_{1}, so d−1<λ1d-1<\lambda_{1}. Since d≠1d\neq 1, the set {c,c+1,…,c+d−1}\{c,c+1,\dots,c+d-1\} has more than one element and it has exactly one multiple of dd. A non-multiple of dd of the form c+ic+i with 0≤i≤d−10\leq i\leq d-1 cannot be generated by {λ1,…,λc−g−1}∪{c,c+1,…,c+i−1}\{\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{c-g-1}\}\cup\{c,c+1,\dots,c+i-1\}. Indeed, let ℛ={c,c+1,…,c+i−1}\mathcal{R}=\{c,c+1,\dots,c+i-1\}. Suppose that c+i=λj1+⋯+λjkc+i=\lambda_{j_{1}}+\dots+\lambda_{j_{k}}. But none of the λjs\lambda_{j_{s}} is in ℛ\mathcal{R} since, otherwise, if λjs∈ℛ\lambda_{j_{s}}\in\mathcal{R}, then λjs≥c\lambda_{j_{s}}\geq c, and so c+i−λjs≤i≤d−1<λ1c+i-\lambda_{j_{s}}\leq i\leq d-1<\lambda_{1}, a contradiction. Therefore, every numerical semigroup that is in an infinite chain has at least d−1d-1 children. Moreover, if λ1=d\lambda_{1}=d, then, by Proposition 2.2, Λ\Lambda has exactly d−1d-1 effective generators. ∎

Definition 4.6.

A numerical semigroup is fertile if most of its children are in infinite chains.

Proposition 4.7.

A numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda is fertile if and only if one of the options below holds:

  1. a.

    Λ=ℕ0\Lambda=\mathbb{N}_{0};

  2. b.

    Λ\Lambda is a hyperelliptic semigroup;

  3. c.

    h⁡(Λ)=3h(\Lambda)=3 and two of its children are in infinite chains.

Proof.

Let Λ\Lambda be a fertile numerical semigroup. By Corollary 4.1, if h⁡(Λ)>3h(\Lambda)>3 then it has at most 22 children in infinite chains, so it cannot be fertile. If h⁡(Λ)=3h(\Lambda)=3, then it is fertile if it has 22 children in infinite chains, which corresponds to the case c. If h⁡(Λ)=2h(\Lambda)=2, then Λ\Lambda is fertile if both its children are in infinite chains and, by Proposition 4.3, that occurs when Λ=ℕ0∖{1}\Lambda=\mathbb{N}_{0}\setminus\{1\}, which is hyperelliptic as desired. Finally, if h⁡(Λ)=1h(\Lambda)=1 and its only child is in an infinite chain, then Λ\Lambda is a hyperelliptic semigroup or ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0}. ∎

There is one hyperelliptic semigroup at each level and we would like to explore what is the frequency of numerical semigroups of type c at each level of the semigroup tree. Consider the semigroup sequence defined by Mn:={4k:k≥0}∪[4n+2,∞)M_{n}:=\{4k:k\geq 0\}\cup[4n+2,\infty).

Note that, if Λ=Mn\Lambda=M_{n} for some n≥1n\geq 1, then c⁡(Λ)=4​n+2c(\Lambda)=4n+2 is a minimal generator of Λ\Lambda, gcd(ℒ⁡(Λ))=(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda))= gcd(0,4,…,4​n)=4(0,4,\dots,4n)=4 and gcd(ℒ⁡(Λ∖{c⁡(Λ)+1}))=(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda\setminus\{c(\Lambda)+1\}))= gcd(ℒ⁡(Λ),4​n+2)=2(\mathcal{L}(\Lambda),4n+2)=2. So, by Theorem 3.4, Λ∖{c}\Lambda\setminus\{c\} and Λ∖{c+1}\Lambda\setminus\{c+1\} are in infinite chains. In addition, c⁡(Λ)+3=4​n+5c(\Lambda)+3=4n+5 is also an effective generator and, by Proposition 2.2, it is the last of them. Therefore, Λ=Mn\Lambda=M_{n} is of type c.

Proposition 4.8.

A numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda of genus g>2g>2 is of type c if and only if Λ=Mn\Lambda=M_{n} for some n≥1n\geq 1, where Mn={4k:k≥0}∪[4n+2,∞)M_{n}=\{4k:k\geq 0\}\cup[4n+2,\infty).

Proof.

The only ordinary numerical semigroup which is of type c has genus 22 since the number of effective generators of the ordinary semigroup of genus gg is g+1g+1, while type c semigroups have efficacy equal to 3. Let Λ\Lambda be a numerical semigroup of type c, and let g=g⁡(Λ)>2,c=c⁡(Λ)g=g(\Lambda)>2,c=c(\Lambda) be its genus and conductor and let λ\lambda be its enumeration. Then, gcd(λ0,…,λc−g−1)=d>1(\lambda_{0},\dots,\lambda_{c-g-1})=d>1 and, since h⁡(Λ)=3h(\Lambda)=3, by Lemma 4.5, we have d≤4d\leq 4. Moreover, by Remark 4.2, cc and c+1c+1 are generators of Λ\Lambda, with gcd(λ0,…,λc−g−1,λc−g)=d′>1(\lambda_{0},\dots,\lambda_{c-g-1},\lambda_{c-g})=d^{\prime}>1.

If d=2d=2, then d′=2d^{\prime}=2, cc is even, and λ1≠2\lambda_{1}\neq 2 by Lemma 4.5. In this case, all nongaps before c+1c+1 are even, so if c+3c+3 is not a generator, 2∈Λ2\in\Lambda, which is a contradiction. Thus c+3c+3 is the largest effective generator and the only possibility to write c+5c+5 as the sum of nongaps is c+5=(c+1)+4c+5=(c+1)+4. Then, 4∈Λ4\in\Lambda and cc must be congruent to 22 modulo 44, in order to be a generator. Now, since d≠4d\neq 4, there must exist λi∈ℒ⁡(Λ)\lambda_{i}\in\mathcal{L}(\Lambda) such that 4∤λi4\nmid\lambda_{i}. That is, λi\lambda_{i} is congruent to 22 modulo 44. But then c−λic-\lambda_{i} is a multiple of 44, and so it belongs to Λ\Lambda, contradicting the fact that cc is a generator.

If d=3d=3, similarly we have 3|c3\mid c, and so 3∤c+23\nmid c+2. Thus, c+2c+2 is not equal to the sum of any elements of Λ\Lambda smaller than cc, so c+2c+2 is the third effective generator. Consequently c,c+1,c+2c,c+1,c+2 are the three effective generators of Λ\Lambda and, since c+4c+4 is not multiple of 33 and it is not a generator, writing c+4c+4 as the sum of nongaps we get c+4=(c+1)+3c+4=(c+1)+3 or c+4=(c+2)+2c+4=(c+2)+2. So, either 2∈Λ2\in\Lambda or 3∈Λ3\in\Lambda but 2∈Λ2\in\Lambda contradicts d=3d=3 and 3∈Λ3\in\Lambda contradicts cc being a generator.

If d=4d=4 and m>4m>4, then cc is even because d′|4d^{\prime}\mid 4 and d′≠1d^{\prime}\neq 1. Thus, c+3c+3 and c+5c+5 are odd, and so they are generators of Λ\Lambda, contradicting h⁡(Λ)=3h(\Lambda)=3.

If d=4d=4 and m=4m=4, then all left elements are multiples of 44, and cc needs to be even and not multiple of 44 since we have d′≠1d^{\prime}\neq 1 and cc a generator. This description corresponds exactly to the semigroups of the sequence MnM_{n}. ∎

It is easy to see that g⁡(Mn)=3​n+1g(M_{n})=3n+1. Thus we obtain the following result.

Theorem 4.9.

The unique fertile semigroups of genus gg are:

  1. a.

    ℕ0{\mathbb{N}}_{0} if g=0g=0.

  2. b.

    ℕ0∖{1}{\mathbb{N}}_{0}\setminus\{1\} if g=1g=1.

  3. c.

    ℋg\mathcal{H}_{g} if g>1g>1 and g≢1mod3g\not\equiv 1\mod 3.

  4. d.

    ℋg\mathcal{H}_{g} and Mg−13M_{\frac{g-1}{3}} if g>1g>1 and g≡1mod3g\equiv 1\mod 3.

Proof.

Direct from Propositions 4.7 and 4.8. ∎

Let igi_{g} be the number of numerical semigroups of genus gg that are in an infinite chain.

Theorem 4.10.

For g≥5g\geq 5 we have ig≤12​ngi_{g}\leq\dfrac{1}{2}n_{g}.

Proof.

Computations show that i5=6i_{5}=6 and n5=12n_{5}=12. For fixed g≥6g\geq 6, let us prove that there are more numerical semigroups with genus gg that are not in infinite chains than the other way around. To do so, we partition the set of numerical semigroups of genus gg into three disjoint sets:

Fg\displaystyle F_{g} :={Λ:g⁡(Λ)=g​ and ​Λ∪{F⁡(Λ)}​ is fertile}\displaystyle:=\{\Lambda:g(\Lambda)=g\text{ and }\Lambda\cup\{F(\Lambda)\}\text{ is fertile}\}
Og\displaystyle O_{g} :={Λ:g⁡(Λ)=g​ and ​Λ∪{F⁡(Λ)}​ is ordinary}\displaystyle:=\{\Lambda:g(\Lambda)=g\text{ and }\Lambda\cup\{F(\Lambda)\}\text{ is ordinary}\}
Pg\displaystyle P_{g} :={Λ:g⁡(Λ)=g​ and ​Λ∉Fg⊔Og}\displaystyle:=\{\Lambda:g(\Lambda)=g\text{ and }\Lambda\notin F_{g}\sqcup O_{g}\}

By Lemma 4.4, Pg≠∅P_{g}\neq\emptyset. By Theorem 4.9 at most half the nodes in PgP_{g} lie in an infinite chain.

If g−1≡1mod3g-1\equiv 1\mod 3 then, by Theorem 4.9, there exist 33 numerical semigroups in FgF_{g} which are in an infinite chain and 11 which is not. In OgO_{g} there are 22 elements in an infinite chain and g−2≥4g-2\geq 4 that are not. In this way, the difference between the number of elements of Fg⊔OgF_{g}\sqcup O_{g} which are not in an infinite chain and the number of those that are is non-negative as well. If g−1≢1mod3g-1\not\equiv 1\mod 3, then FgF_{g} has only 11 element and it belongs to an infinite chain and the result holds similarly. ∎

5 Fixing the multiplicity

In the tree that organizes all semigroups by genus, the set of descendants of ℕ0∖{1,3}\mathbb{N}_{0}\setminus\{1,3\} is a single infinite chain of hyperelliptic semigroups. Indeed, ℕ0∖{1,3}\mathbb{N}_{0}\setminus\{1,3\} is the third semigroup in IℋI_{\mathcal{H}}. On the other hand ℕ0∖{1,2}\mathbb{N}_{0}\setminus\{1,2\} is in I𝒪I_{\mathcal{O}}, the infinite chain formed by the ordinary semigroups. From each ordinary semigroup in I𝒪I_{\mathcal{O}} there emerges a subtree that contains all the semigroups of the same multiplicity (as one can see in [5]). From now on, we focus on these subtrees with fixed multiplicity. One way to transit in such a subtree is, from a semigroup in it, to move to another numerical semigroup of higher genus while maintaining the structure of the first semigroup, that is, maintaining the structure of its non-gaps. The construction explained in next definition does this: it pushes the non-gaps of a numerical semigroup while keeping its multiplicity.

Definition 5.1.

The push of a numerical semigroup Λ\Lambda, with enumeration λ\lambda, by its multiplicity is λ1⊕Λ:={0}∪{λ1+λj;λj∈Λ}.\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda:=\{0\}\cup\{\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{j};\lambda_{j}\in\Lambda\}.

The set λ1⊕Λ\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda as above is a numerical semigroup. In fact, if x,y∈λ1⊕Λx,y\in\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda then, either x,yx,y or both are zero, in which case the sum belongs to λ1⊕Λ\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda, or there exist λa,λb∈Λ\lambda_{a},\lambda_{b}\in\Lambda such that x=λ1+λax=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{a} and y=λ1+λby=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{b}. In this case, x+y=λ1+(λa+λ1+λb)∈λ1⊕Λx+y=\lambda_{1}+(\lambda_{a}+\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{b})\in\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda. In addition, if x≥λ1+c⁡(Λ)x\geq\lambda_{1}+c(\Lambda), then x−λ1∈Λx-\lambda_{1}\in\Lambda, and so x∈λ1⊕Λx\in\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda. That is, λ1+c⁡(Λ)−1\lambda_{1}+c(\Lambda)-1 is the maximum of (λ1⊕Λ)C(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)^{C} and, thus, (λ1⊕Λ)C(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)^{C} is finite. Moreover, m⁡(λ1⊕Λ)=λ1m(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)=\lambda_{1}, g⁡(λ1⊕Λ)=g⁡(Λ)+λ1−1g(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)=g(\Lambda)+\lambda_{1}-1, c⁡(λ1⊕Λ)=λ1+c⁡(Λ)c(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)=\lambda_{1}+c(\Lambda), ℒ⁡(λ1⊕Λ)={0}∪{λ1+λj;λj∈ℒ⁡(Λ)}\mathcal{L}(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)=\{0\}\cup\{\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{j};\lambda_{j}\in\mathcal{L}(\Lambda)\} and #​ℒ​(λ1⊕Λ)=#​ℒ​(Λ)+1\#\mathcal{L}(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)=\#\mathcal{L}(\Lambda)+1.

Lemma 5.2.

Let Λ\Lambda be a numerical semigroup with enumeration λ\lambda and let Π\Pi be a non-ordinary numerical semigroup. Then,

  1. a.

    If λk\lambda_{k} is an (effective) generator of Λ\Lambda, then λ1+λk\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{k} is an (effective) generator of λ1⊕Λ\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda.

  2. b.

    Π\Pi is a child of Λ\Lambda if and only if λ1⊕Π\lambda_{1}\oplus\Pi is a child of λ1⊕Λ\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda.

  3. c.

    Λ\Lambda lies in an infinite chain if and only if so does λ1⊕Λ\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda.

Proof.

Direct by Definition 5.1. ∎

The reciprocal of implication a is not true in general. For instance, ⟨4,5,6⟩\langle 4,5,6\rangle is a leaf, while 4⊕⟨4,5,6⟩4\oplus\langle 4,5,6\rangle is a stick. From now on, we use the notation λ1⊕nΛ\lambda_{1}\oplus^{n}\Lambda to represent λ1⊕(⋯(λ1⊕(λ1⊕Λ)))⏟n​ times\underbrace{\lambda_{1}\oplus(\cdots(\lambda_{1}\oplus(\lambda_{1}\oplus\Lambda)))}_{n\text{ times}}.

Now we will investigate infinite chains in subtrees with some fixed multiplicity. We call infinite chains of multiplicity mm those infinite chains whose first mm semigroups are the ordinary semigroups of multiplicities 11 to mm and after that all semigroups in the chain have multiplicity mm. Equivalently, an infinite chain is an infinite chain of multiplicity mm if and only if the maximum of the multiplicities of the semigroups in the chain is mm.

5.1 Prime multiplicity

From Theorem 3.4 one can deduce that, for each prime multiplicity, there is only one infinite chain of that multiplicity. Indeed, this unique chain is ω⁡(m,ℕ0)\omega(m,{\mathbb{N}}_{0}). Hence, we can state the following theorem.

Theorem 5.3.

If mm is a prime, then the number ig​(m)i_{g}(m) of numerical semigroups of genus g≥m−1g\geq m-1 and multiplicity mm that are in an infinite chain is 11.

5.2 Multiplicity 4

The tree in Figure 2 represents the numerical semigroups of multiplicity 44, genus from 33 to 55 and which are in infinite chains. The edges connect semigroups as usual, being a child of a given semigroup the given semigroup minus one of its effective generators.

Specifically: A={0,4,→},B={0,4,6,→},C={0,4,7,→}A=\{0,4,\rightarrow\},B=\{0,4,6,\rightarrow\},C=\{0,4,7,\rightarrow\}, and D={0,4,6,8,→}D=\{0,4,6,8,\rightarrow\}.

As we can observe, c⁡(C)c(C) is a generator while c⁡(C)+1c(C)+1 is not. So by Remark 4.2 CC has only one child in an infinite chain and this child is exactly 4⊕A4\oplus A. In general, for n≥1n\geq 1, 4⊕nC∖{c(4⊕nC)}=4⊕n+1A4\oplus^{n}C\setminus\{c(4\oplus^{n}C)\}=4\oplus^{n+1}A is the only child of 4⊕nC4\oplus^{n}C that is in an infinite chain. Moreover, 4⊕nA4\oplus^{n}A has one child in an infinite chain, and so by Lemma 5.2 this child is 4⊕nB4\oplus^{n}B.

On the other hand, the efficacy of 4⊕nD={0,4,⋯,4n,4n+2,4n+4,→}4\oplus^{n}D=\{0,4,\cdots,4n,4n+2,4n+4,\rightarrow\}, with n≥1n\geq 1, is equal to 22. So the efficacy of any descendant of 4⊕nD4\oplus^{n}D is at most 22. Then by Proposition 4.3 every descendant of 4⊕nD4\oplus^{n}D has exactly one child in an infinite chain. So, the infinite chain emerging from a node of the form 4⊕nD4\oplus^{n}D is made of sticks in the tree of semigroups that are in infinite chains. In that way we have the following theorem.

Theorem 5.4.

The number ig​(4)i_{g}(4) of numerical semigroups of genus g≥3g\geq 3 and multiplicity 44 that are in an infinite chain is

⌊g+13⌋.\left\lfloor\dfrac{g+1}{3}\right\rfloor.
Proof.

It is clear for g=3,4g=3,4. Otherwise, the tree in Figure 2 is self-replicated in the tree of infinite chains of multiplicity 44 starting at {0,4,→}\{0,4,\rightarrow\}. Moreover, as observed before, the numerical semigroups of multiplicity 44 that are in an infinite chain and do not participate in self-replication are sticks in the tree of semigroups that are in infinite chains. ∎

In the tree in Figure 3 we can observe thirteen complete self-replications of the tree in Figure 2. The figure was generated with the drawsgtree tool [4], by command ./drawsgtree -g41 -m4 -e infinitechains -etrim -d .2.

5.3 Multiplicity 6

The numerical semigroup of multiplicity 66 and with the smallest genus is the ordinary semigroup {0,6,→}\{0,6,\rightarrow\}. It has two children in infinite chains: the ordinary semigroup {0,7,→}\{0,7,\rightarrow\} and the semigroup {0,6,8,→}\{0,6,8,\rightarrow\}. To study the numerical semigroups that are in infinite chains and have multiplicity 66, we study the tree υ\upsilon formed by {0,6,→}\{0,6,\rightarrow\} in its root and connected to {0,6,8,→}\{0,6,8,\rightarrow\} and all semigroups descending from it that are in infinite chains. In other words, υ\upsilon is formed by the subtree rooted at {0,6,→}\{0,6,\rightarrow\} that contains all numerical semigroups in infinite chains, where the node {0,7,→}\{0,7,\rightarrow\} and all its descendants have been trimmed.

The semigroups of υ\upsilon are of type Λn={0,6,…,6n,6n+β1,…,6n+βj,→}\Lambda_{n}=\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+\beta_{1},\dots,6n+\beta_{j},\rightarrow\}. In this case we can use the jj-tuple (β1​…,βj)n(\beta_{1}\dots,\beta_{j})_{n} to represent Λn\Lambda_{n}. For example, we represent {0,6,8,→}\{0,6,8,\rightarrow\} by (2)1(2)_{1} and {0,6,12,14,16,18,20,22,24,→}\{0,6,12,14,16,18,20,22,24,\rightarrow\} by (2,4,6,8,10,12)2(2,4,6,8,10,12)_{2}. We use (⋅)n(\cdot)_{n} to represent the ordinary semigroup of genus 6​n−16n-1.

5.3.1 The tree τn\tau_{n} and its replications

In Table 1 we have thirteen numerical semigroups that have multiplicity 66, are in infinite chains and have some parenting relationships that can be observed in the tree τn\tau_{n} in Figure 4. By Remark 4.2 and the last column in Table 1, we verify that each semigroup Λn\Lambda_{n} in τn\tau_{n} has children in infinite chains as drawn in Figure 2.

Note that InI_{n} has only one child in an infinite chain which is In∖{c⁡(In)}=6⊕AnI_{n}\setminus\{c(I_{n})\}=6\oplus A_{n}. Moreover, 6⊕Λn=Λn+16\oplus\Lambda_{n}=\Lambda_{n+1} for all n≥1n\geq 1 and Λn\Lambda_{n} a numerical semigroup from Table 1. Therefore, the finite tree in Figure 4 is self-replicated in υ\upsilon through push by multiplicity.

5.3.2 Outside the replications of τn\tau_{n}

Now we focus on the numerical semigroups of multiplicity 66 that are in an infinite chain and do not participate in that self-replication, i.e., the descendants of Jn,Kn,LnJ_{n},K_{n},L_{n}, and MnM_{n}.

Proposition 5.6.

The numerical semigroups Kn={0,6,…,6n,6n+3,6n+6,→}K_{n}=\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+3,6n+6,\rightarrow\} and Mn={0,6,…,6n,6n+2,6n+4,6n+6,6n+8,→}M_{n}=\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+2,6n+4,6n+6,6n+8,\rightarrow\} each belong to one infinite chain.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.4 the number of infinite chains to which KnK_{n} belongs is one plus the number of descendants of K~n={0,2,…,2n,2n+1,2n+2,→}\tilde{K}_{n}=\{0,2,\dots,2n,2n+1,2n+2,\rightarrow\} beyond 2​n+12n+1. But K~n\tilde{K}_{n} has no generators larger than 2​n+12n+1, and so it has no descendants beyond 2​n+12n+1. Thus, KnK_{n} only belongs to one infinite chain.

Similarly, the number of infinite chains to which MnM_{n} belongs is one plus the number of descendants of M~n={0,3,…,3n,3n+1,3n+2,3n+3,3n+4,→}\tilde{M}_{n}=\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+1,3n+2,3n+3,3n+4,\rightarrow\} beyond 3​n+33n+3. But M~n\tilde{M}_{n} has no generators larger than 3​n+33n+3, and so it has no descendants beyond 3​n+33n+3. Thus, MnM_{n} only belongs to one infinite chain. ∎

Proposition 5.7.

The numerical semigroups Jn={0,6,…,6n,6n+4,6n+6,→}J_{n}=\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+4,6n+6,\rightarrow\} belong to n+1n+1 infinite chains.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.4, the number of infinite chains in which JnJ_{n} lies is one plus the number of descendants of J~n={0,3,…,3n,3n+2,3n+3,→}\tilde{J}_{n}=\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+2,3n+3,\rightarrow\} beyond 3​n+23n+2.

If n=1n=1, J~n\tilde{J}_{n} has one descendant beyond 55. Hence, J1J_{1} lies in two infinite chains.

Suppose n>1n>1. Observe that J~n\tilde{J}_{n} has one unique child that contains {0,3,…,3​n,3​n+2}\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+2\}, which is J~n∖{3​n+4}\tilde{J}_{n}\setminus\{3n+4\}. Observe also that any semigroup containing {0,3,…,3​n,3​n+2}\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+2\} must contain the semigroup

{0,3,…,3n,3n+1,3(n+1),3(n+1)+2…,3(2n),3(2n)+2,→}.\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+1,3(n+1),3(n+1)+2\dots,3(2n),3(2n)+2,\rightarrow\}.

One can deduce that all descendants of J~n\tilde{J}_{n} beyond 3​n+23n+2 are exactly the semigroups J~n,t={0,3,…,3n,3n+2,3(n+1),3(n+1)+2,…,3(n+t),3(n+t)+2,→}\tilde{J}_{n,t}=\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+2,3(n+1),3(n+1)+2,\dots,3(n+t),3(n+t)+2,\rightarrow\} for 2≤t≤n+12\leq t\leq n+1. Hence, JnJ_{n} lies in exactly n+1n+1 infinite chains. ∎

Proposition 5.8.

The numerical semigroups Ln={0,6,…,6n,6n+2,6n+6,→}L_{n}=\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+2,6n+6,\rightarrow\} belong to nn infinite chains.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.4, the number of infinite chains in which LnL_{n} lies is one plus the number of descendants of L~n={0,3,…,3n,3n+1,3n+3,→}\tilde{L}_{n}=\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+1,3n+3,\rightarrow\} beyond 3​n+13n+1.

If n=1n=1, L~n\tilde{L}_{n} has no descendants beyond 44. Hence, L1L_{1} lies in exactly one infinite chain.

Suppose n>1n>1. Observe that L~n\tilde{L}_{n} has one unique child, which is L~n∖{3​n+4}\tilde{L}_{n}\setminus\{3n+4\}. Observe also that any semigroup containing {0,3,…,3​n,3​n+1}\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+1\} must contain the semigroup

{0,3,…,3n,3n+1,3(n+1),3(n+1)+1…,3(2n),3(2n)+1,3(2n)+2,→}.\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+1,3(n+1),3(n+1)+1\dots,3(2n),3(2n)+1,3(2n)+2,\rightarrow\}.

One can deduce that all descendants of L~n\tilde{L}_{n} beyond 3​n+13n+1 are exactly the semigroups L~n,t={0,3,…,3n,3n+1,3(n+1),3(n+1)+1,…,3(n+t),3(n+t)+1,→}\tilde{L}_{n,t}=\{0,3,\dots,3n,3n+1,3(n+1),3(n+1)+1,\dots,3(n+t),3(n+t)+1,\rightarrow\} for 2≤t≤n2\leq t\leq n. Hence, LnL_{n} lies in exactly nn infinite chains. ∎

In order to know at which levels of the tree of numerical semigroups the descendants of the semigroups JnJ_{n} and LnL_{n} has two children in infinite chains, let us define in the next two lemmas some numerical semigroups.

Lemma 5.9.

For every integer tt with 1≤t≤n1\leq t\leq n, the set

γn,t\displaystyle\gamma_{n,t} =\displaystyle= {0,6,…,6n,6n+4,7n,7n+4,…,6(n+t−1),6(n+t−1)+4,\displaystyle\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+4,7n,7n+4,\dots,6(n+t-1),6(n+t-1)+4,
6(n+t),6(n+t)+2,→}\displaystyle\phantom{mmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmm}6(n+t),6(n+t)+2,\rightarrow\}
=\displaystyle= {0,6,…,6n,6n+a1,6n+a2,…,6n+a2​t+1,→},\displaystyle\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+a_{1},6n+a_{2},\dots,6n+a_{2t+1},\rightarrow\},

with

ai={3​i+1if ​i​ is odd and ​i≠2​t+13​i,if ​i​ is even3​i−1,if ​i=2​t+1.a_{i}=\begin{cases}3i+1&\text{if }i\text{ is odd and }i\neq 2t+1\\ 3i,&\text{if }i\text{ is even}\\ 3i-1,&\text{if }i=2t+1.\end{cases}

satisfies:

  1. a.

    γn,t\gamma_{n,t} is a numerical semigroup.

  2. b.

    γn,1\gamma_{n,1} is a child of JnJ_{n} and, for t≥2t\geq 2, γn,t\gamma_{n,t} is a descendant of JnJ_{n}.

  3. c.

    If t≤nt\leq n, then γn,t\gamma_{n,t} has two children in infinite chains.

  4. d.

    The semigroups JnJ_{n}, γn,1,γn,2\gamma_{n,1},\gamma_{n,2}, …,γn,n\gamma_{n,n} are in the same infinite chain.

  5. e.

    The genus of γn,t\gamma_{n,t} is 5​n+4​t+15n+4t+1.

The proof is straightforward and is left to the reader.

Let ζn\zeta_{n} be the infinite chain where all the semigroups {Jn,γn,t}1≤t≤n\{J_{n},\gamma_{n,t}\}_{1\leq t\leq n} of Lemma 5.9 belong. Since each γn,t\gamma_{n,t} has two children in infinite chains, one child belongs to ζn\zeta_{n} and the other one belongs to a different infinite chain. Thus, the n+1n+1 infinite chains from Proposition 5.8 to which SnS_{n} belongs are ζn\zeta_{n} and nn other chains, each of them containing γt,n∖{c⁡(γt,n)+1}\gamma_{t,n}\setminus\{c(\gamma_{t,n})+1\}, for tt between 11 and nn.

Lemma 5.10.

For every integer tt with 1≤t≤n−11\leq t\leq n-1, the set

=\displaystyle= {0,6,…,6n,6n+b1,6n+b2,…,6n+b2​t+2,→},\displaystyle\{0,6,\dots,6n,6n+b_{1},6n+b_{2},\dots,6n+b_{2t+2},\rightarrow\},

with

bi={3​i−1if ​i​ is odd3​i,if ​i​ is even and​i≠2​t+23​i−2,if ​i=2​t+2.b_{i}=\begin{cases}3i-1&\text{if }i\text{ is odd}\\ 3i,&\text{if }i\text{ is even and}i\neq 2t+2\\ 3i-2,&\text{if }i=2t+2.\end{cases}

  2. b.

Let ηn\eta_{n} be the infinite chain where all the semigroups {Ln,νn,t}1≤t≤n−1\{L_{n},\nu_{n,t}\}_{1\leq t\leq n-1} of Lemma 5.10 belong. For nn fixed, since each νn,t\nu_{n,t} have two children in infinite chains, one child belongs to ηn\eta_{n} and the other one belongs to a different infinite chain. Thus, the nn infinite chains from Proposition 5.8 to which LnL_{n} belongs are ηn\eta_{n} and n−1n-1 other chains, each one containing νt,n∖{c⁡(νt,n)+1}\nu_{t,n}\setminus\{c(\nu_{t,n})+1\}, for tt between 11 and n−1n-1.

5.3.3 Growth of the tree υ\upsilon

In Figure 5 we draw the edges and nodes of υ\upsilon corresponding to semigroups from genus 55 up to genus 2929. The tree τ3\tau_{3} and the infinite chains ζ3\zeta_{3} and η3\eta_{3} are highlighted. Notice also that one can observe five full self-replications of the tree from Figure 4. The figure was generated with the drawsgtree tool [4] with the command ./drawsgtree -g29 -m6 -e infinitechains -etrim -d .1.

The number ig​(6)i_{g}(6) of numerical semigroups of genus gg and multiplicity 66 that are in an infinite chain whenever g≥5g\geq 5, is equal to the number of numerical semigroups on level g−5g-5 of the tree υ\upsilon. From what has been developed in Subsection 5.3, the growth of the tree υ\upsilon is known and we are ready to state it in the next theorem.

The number ig​(6)i_{g}(6) of numerical semigroups of genus g≥5g\geq 5 and multiplicity 66 that are in an infinite chain is

{g−5−⌊g−55⌋+∑n=1⌊g−29⌋n+∑n=⌊g+79⌋⌊g−65⌋⌊g−2−5​n4⌋+∑n=2⌊g+19⌋(n−1)+∑n=⌊g+109⌋⌊g−75⌋⌊g−3−5​n4⌋if ​g≡1,2mod5,g−4−⌊g−55⌋+∑n=1⌊g−29⌋n+∑n=⌊g+79⌋⌊g−65⌋⌊g−2−5​n4⌋+∑n=2⌊g+19⌋(n−1)+∑n=⌊g+109⌋⌊g−75⌋⌊g−3−5​n4⌋if ​g≡0,3,4mod5.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}g-5-\left\lfloor\dfrac{g-5}{5}\right\rfloor+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-2}{9}\right\rfloor}n+\sum\limits_{n=\left\lfloor\frac{g+7}{9}\right\rfloor}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-6}{5}\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\dfrac{g-2-5n}{4}\right\rfloor+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g+1}{9}\right\rfloor}(n-1)+\sum\limits_{n=\left\lfloor\frac{g+10}{9}\right\rfloor}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-7}{5}\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\dfrac{g-3-5n}{4}\right\rfloor\\ \mbox{if }g\equiv 1,2\mod 5,\\ g-4-\left\lfloor\dfrac{g-5}{5}\right\rfloor+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-2}{9}\right\rfloor}n+\sum\limits_{n=\left\lfloor\frac{g+7}{9}\right\rfloor}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-6}{5}\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\dfrac{g-2-5n}{4}\right\rfloor+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g+1}{9}\right\rfloor}(n-1)+\sum\limits_{n=\left\lfloor\frac{g+10}{9}\right\rfloor}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-7}{5}\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\dfrac{g-3-5n}{4}\right\rfloor\\ \mbox{if }g\equiv 0,3,4\mod 5.\end{array}\right.
Proof.

First of all, notice that the number of self-replications of the structure of τ1\tau_{1}, from Figure 4, which lie before level g−5g-5 of υ\upsilon is ⌊g−55⌋\lfloor\frac{g-5}{5}\rfloor.

For fixed gg we can define four sets of numerical semigroups:

A\displaystyle A :={Λ:Λ∈τ⌊g−55⌋+1​ and ​g​(Λ)=g}\displaystyle:=\left\{\Lambda:\Lambda\in\tau_{\left\lfloor\frac{g-5}{5}\right\rfloor+1}\text{ and }g(\Lambda)=g\right\}

{Λ:Λ is a descendant of Jn or Ln,1≤n≤⌊g−55⌋,Λ∈ζn∪ηn, and g(Λ)=g}\displaystyle\left\{\Lambda:\Lambda\text{ is a descendant of }J_{n}\text{ or }L_{n},1\leq n\leq\left\lfloor\frac{g-5}{5}\right\rfloor,\Lambda\in\zeta_{n}\cup\eta_{n},\text{ and }g(\Lambda)=g\right\}

D\displaystyle D :={Λ:Λ is a descendant of Ln,2≤n≤⌊g−55⌋,Λ∉ηn, and g(Λ)=g}.\displaystyle:=\left\{\Lambda:\Lambda\text{ is a descendant of }L_{n},2\leq n\leq\left\lfloor\frac{g-5}{5}\right\rfloor,\Lambda\notin\eta_{n},\text{ and }g(\Lambda)=g\right\}.

In the definition of DD the case n=1n=1 has been excluded since L1L_{1} belongs only to one infinite chain which is exactly η1\eta_{1}.

Now, the numerical semigroups of genus g≤5g\leq 5 and multiplicity 66 which are in an infinite chain are the numerical semigroups of A⊔B⊔C⊔DA\sqcup B\sqcup C\sqcup D.

To get the cardinality of AA, consider the remainder rr such that g−5=5​⌊g−55⌋+rg-5=5\lfloor\frac{g-5}{5}\rfloor+r. It is the level of the tree τ⌊g−55⌋+1\tau_{\left\lfloor\frac{g-5}{5}\right\rfloor+1} at which the numerical semigroups of genus gg that participate in self-replication lie. So, the cardinality of AA is equal to rr if r=1,2r=1,2 and equal to r+1r+1 when r=0,3,4r=0,3,4.

By Proposition 5.6, Lemma 5.9, and Lemma 5.10, the cardinality of BB is equal to 4​⌊g−55⌋4\lfloor\frac{g-5}{5}\rfloor.

=∑n=1⌊g−29⌋n+∑n=⌊g+79⌋⌊g−65⌋⌊g−2−5​n4⌋.\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-2}{9}\right\rfloor}n+\sum\limits_{n=\left\lfloor\frac{g+7}{9}\right\rfloor}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-6}{5}\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\frac{g-2-5n}{4}\right\rfloor.

=∑n=2⌊g+19⌋(n−1)+∑n=⌊g+109⌋⌊g−75⌋⌊g−3−5​n4⌋\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g+1}{9}\right\rfloor}(n-1)+\sum\limits_{n=\left\lfloor\frac{g+10}{9}\right\rfloor}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-7}{5}\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\frac{g-3-5n}{4}\right\rfloor
=∑n=1⌊g−89⌋n+∑n=⌊g+109⌋⌊g−75⌋⌊g−3−5​n4⌋.\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-8}{9}\right\rfloor}n+\sum\limits_{n=\left\lfloor\frac{g+10}{9}\right\rfloor}^{\left\lfloor\frac{g-7}{5}\right\rfloor}\left\lfloor\frac{g-3-5n}{4}\right\rfloor.

The anonymous reviewer noticed that the formula given in Lemma 5.11 is nothing else but ig​(6)=⌊2​g2+g−169⌋−⌊(g−1)25⌋.i_{g}(6)=\left\lfloor\frac{2g^{2}+g-16}{9}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{(g-1)^{2}}{5}\right\rfloor. It can be proved by some arguments on quasi-polynomials or using the implementation of Barvinok’s algorithm in LattE [6]. Hence, we can state now the following theorem.

Theorem 5.12.

The number ig​(6)i_{g}(6) of numerical semigroups of genus g≥5g\geq 5 and multiplicity 66 that are in an infinite chain is

ig​(6)=⌊2​g2+g−169⌋−⌊(g−1)25⌋.i_{g}(6)=\left\lfloor\frac{2g^{2}+g-16}{9}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{(g-1)^{2}}{5}\right\rfloor.

6 Open question

Proposition 7 in [8] states that the number of all semigroups of genus gg with fixed multiplicity mm is eventually a quasi-polynomial in gg. The results presented in this work suggest, as pointed out by the anonymous referee, the following conjecture.

Conjecture 6.1.

For a fixed multiplicity mm, the number of semigroups of genus gg lying in an infinite chain is quasi-polynomial in gg, for g≥m−1g\geq m-1.
